prompts.assessment:
# Dataset risk assessment
I would like your help in assessing the likelihood that this data will be changed or removed from its primary location, and that users will no longer be able to access accurate and reliable copies of it, based on the rubric below.

## Sources for context
To help assess the rubric categories, perform additional research on the data, the agency, the data's topics and typical users, covering topics such as proposed regulatory or funding changes, recent news, and political commentary. Use whatever resources you find useful, including the Federal Register (https://www.federalregister.gov) and the federal staffing tracker at https://usajobs-tracker.abigailhaddad.com.

## Rubric
This rubric is divided up into categories. Each category is divided up into risk levels. In your output, please select the appropriate risk level for each category based on your research.

### Historical Data Availability
- Gone: Data files prior to the current year or cycle are no longer publicly available.
- High Risk: Some data files prior to the current year or cycle are removed.
- Moderate Risk: Some data elements that exist in the dataset prior to the current year or cycle are removed.
- No Known Issue: Data prior to the current year or cycle remain accessible with no known alterations.

### Future Data Availability
- Gone: Data collection and publication has been terminated.
- High Risk: Statutory publication deadline missed and/or collection or publication skipped and/or ICR expired for more than one year.
- Moderate Risk: Typical or intended publication date missed and/or collection or publication delayed; ICR expired up to one year.
- No Known Issue: Data published on time or as expected and ICR active or renewed before expiration.

### Data Quality
- Gone: Data collection and publication has been terminated.
- High Risk: Reductions in granularity, timeliness, or frequency.
- Moderate Risk: Potential or emerging risk to granularity, timeliness, or frequency.
- No Known Issue: Maintained or improved granularity, timeliness, or frequency.

### Statutory Context
- Gone: N/A
- High Risk: Statutory authorization is vague and/or there are alternative data collections that could serve as substitutes and/or no known programmatic use.
- Moderate Risk: Not explicitly required by statute but required for the implementation of a state or federal program, and there are no alternative data collections that could serve as substitutes.
- No Known Issue: Statutorily required and/or statutory authorization is explicitly named and it is clear what has to be collected, and there aren't alternative data collections that could serve as substitutes and/or required for implementation of a federal program.

### Staffing and Funding
- Gone: All of the staff in the division or agency are gone and/or all funding has been terminated.
- High Risk: 40% or more of staff lost, and/or 1,000 or more staff lost, and/or budget cut by 20% or more, and/or leadership removed.
- Moderate Risk: 10–39% of staff lost, and/or 500–999 staff lost, and/or budget cut by 10–19%, and/or threatened change in leadership.
- No Known Issue: Less than 10% of staff lost and less than 10% of budget cut and no known change in leadership.

### Policy
- Gone: Data collection and publication has been terminated.
- High Risk: Presidential Action-driven information collection request (ICR); negative policy note on site; other significant changes in accordance with Administration priorities.
- Moderate Risk: Proposed or pending changes; statements by administration officials suggesting a change is being considered or planned.
- No Known Issue: No notable changes since January 2025 affecting what data is collected and published.

For each category, concisely list the evidence and supporting sources that would support each risk level. Then indicate which risk level you find most appropriate and why.

Conclude with a simple summary of risk levels:
Historical Data Availability: <level>
Future Data Availability: <level>
Data Quality: <level>
Statutory Context: <level>
Staffing and Funding: <level>
Policy: <level>

#data research
I am researching a federal dataset. Find out everything you can about this dataset, such as who publishes it, under what authority or mandate, its history, its typical users, and its benefits to the public. Be sure your research comprehensively covers each of those perspectives, as well as any others that you discover or seem useful. I believe this is accurate information, but please check:

Dataset title: Consumer Price Index (CPI)
Description: The Consumer Price Index (CPI) is a measure of the average change over time in the prices paid by urban consumers for a market basket of consumer goods and services. Indexes are available for the U.S. and various geographic areas. Average price data for select utility, automotive fuel, and food items are also available.
URL: https://bls.gov/cpi

Return a complete report on everything that a preservationist, data librarian, data scientist, or policy activist might want to know about this data.

# Research Report: The U.S. Consumer Price Index (CPI)

**Verdict on the supplied description:** Accurate. The title, description, and URL match the Bureau of Labor Statistics' official CPI program page (https://www.bls.gov/cpi). The description is essentially verbatim from BLS's own overview. One clarification worth noting: the "average price data" component (gasoline, electricity, natural gas, and selected food items) is a companion dataset published alongside the indexes, not the index itself.

---

## 1. Publisher and Institutional Context

| Attribute | Detail |
|---|---|
| **Publisher** | U.S. Bureau of Labor Statistics (BLS), Division of Consumer Prices and Price Indexes |
| **Parent agency** | U.S. Department of Labor |
| **Agency type** | One of the 13 principal statistical agencies of the U.S. federal statistical system |
| **Program URL** | https://www.bls.gov/cpi |
| **Publication frequency** | Monthly (national release typically ~8:30 a.m. ET, mid-month, covering the prior month) |
| **Free?** | Yes — all CPI data and documentation are in the public domain and free of charge |

The CPI is one of BLS's flagship programs, alongside the Employment Situation statistics, the Consumer Expenditure Survey (which supplies CPI weights), and the Producer Price Index. BLS itself dates its institutional lineage to 1884 (Bureau of Labor), becoming the Bureau of Labor Statistics when the Department of Labor was created in 1913 (Act of March 4, 1913).

The CPI has unusually high visibility for a statistical product: each monthly release moves financial markets, and BLS briefs the President's economic advisors, Congress, and the Federal Reserve on it. Because it triggers automatic statutory payments (see §6), the release process operates under strict embargo and pre-release access rules coordinated with the Executive Office of the President.

## 2. Legal Authority and Mandate

The CPI is produced under BLS's general statutory authority — there is no single "CPI Act":

- **29 U.S.C. §1** — charges BLS with acquiring and diffusing useful information on subjects connected with labor.
- **29 U.S.C. §2** — directs BLS (under the Secretary of Labor) to "collect, collate, and report at least once each year" statistics on labor conditions; this monthly statistical collection authority underpins the CPI's continuous price collection.
- **Specific downstream mandates** — Congress has repeatedly *used* the CPI by statute and occasionally *directed* BLS to create CPI variants:
  - **Public Law 92-336 (1972)** amended the Social Security Act to provide automatic annual cost-of-living adjustments (COLAs) based on the CPI (first paid 1975) — codified at 42 U.S.C. §415(i).
  - **Public Law 100-175, §191 (1987)** explicitly directed the Secretary of Labor, through BLS, to develop a reweighted index for Americans 62 and older — the origin of the experimental **CPI-E**.
  - **Revenue Act / IRC §1(f)** requires annual inflation adjustment of federal income tax brackets (using the **Chained CPI (C-CPI-U)** since 2018; the CPI-U previously).
  - **Treasury Inflation-Protected Securities (TIPS)** are indexed to the non-seasonally adjusted CPI-U by statute/treasury regulation.
- **Oversight framework**: As a principal federal statistical agency, BLS operates under the **Paperwork Reduction Act**, **Confidential Information Protection and Statistical Efficiency Act (CIPSEA, 2002)** (protecting respondent confidentiality — collected prices and outlet identities are confidential statistical information), OMB statistical policy directives, and information-quality guidelines.
- **Important governance principle**: BLS calculates the CPI but does *not* determine how it is used by other agencies. Whether Social Security uses CPI-W, whether SNAP thresholds follow it, etc., are decisions of Congress and the administering agencies. BLS guards this boundary fiercely for independence.

## 3. History

- **Pre-1913 origins**: Late-19th-century BLS "food price" bulletins (BLS Bulletins on retail prices, e.g., #61 on prices in 1890–92) are the ancestral dataset. The famous 1901 "cost of living" study conducted for the Industrial Commission was a forerunner.
- **1917–1919**: WWI inflation in shipbuilding centers made a comprehensive index essential for cost-of-living wage adjustments in defense industries. BLS conducted family expenditure surveys in 92 industrial centers and began periodic price collection.
- **1919**: BLS began publishing separate indexes for 32 cities. **1921**: regular publication of the national "U.S. city average" began, estimated **back to 1913** — the year BLS treats as the CPI's start. Official continuous monthly data exist from 1913 to the present, making it one of the longest continuous federal economic time series.
- **1920s–1940s**: The index was long known as the "cost-of-living index"; in 1945 it was renamed the **Consumers' Price Index for Moderate Income Families in Large Cities**.
- **1961**: The Stigler Committee (Price Statistics Review Committee, NBER) critiqued the CPI as not a true cost-of-living index — recommendations that shaped decades of methodology work.
- **1978**: Major revision introduced the **CPI-U** (All Urban Consumers) and renamed the older population series the **CPI-W** (Urban Wage Earners and Clerical Workers). Rental-equivalence concepts were developed; in 1983 the housing component shifted from home-purchase/asset prices to **owners' equivalent rent (OER)**.
- **1985**: Federal income tax brackets began being indexed to the CPI.
- **1996**: The **Boskin Commission** (Senate Finance-appointed Advisory Commission to Study the Consumer Price Index) concluded the CPI overstated inflation by ~1.1 percentage points/year (range 0.8–1.6), with major federal budget implications. BLS responded with methodological changes (see §8).
- **1999**: Geometric mean formula adopted for most basic-level indexes; **CPI-U-RS** (research series incorporating historical improvements) introduced; new housing survey from the 1990 census.
- **2002**: **Chained CPI (C-CPI-U)** added using the Törnqvist "superlative" formula to correct upper-level substitution bias; biennial (now annual) weight updates began.
- **2008**: CPI-E published retroactively to 1982 (experimental).
- **2018–present**: Geographic sample redesigned on the 2010 census (32 index areas); weights updated annually from the Consumer Expenditure Survey; ongoing "weight/time-lag" improvements accelerated after the 2021–22 inflation episode.

A detailed **"Chronology of changes in the Consumer Price Index"** (bls.gov/cpi/additional-resources/historical-changes.htm) documents every methodological change — a critical resource for longitudinal research.

## 4. What the Dataset Contains

**Index populations:**
- **CPI-U** — all urban consumers (~93% of the U.S. population); the headline, most-used index.
- **CPI-W** — urban wage earners and clerical workers (~30% of the population); used for Social Security COLAs and many union contracts.
- **C-CPI-U** — chained index for the CPI-U population; national-level only; issued as preliminary and subject to up to three quarterly revisions (unlike CPI-U/CPI-W, which are final at release).
- **Research/experimental indexes**: R-CPI-E (elderly), R-CPI-I and R-C-CPI-I (income quintiles), CPI-U-RS (retrospective historical research series).

**Geographic coverage:** U.S. city average; 4 census regions and 9 divisions; city-size classes; and 23 selected metropolitan areas (e.g., New York, Los Angeles, Chicago). Note the CPI covers **urban areas only** — rural consumers, farm households, military installations, and institutional populations are excluded by design.

**Item coverage:** The market basket spans roughly 211 item strata aggregated into 8 major groups (food and beverages, housing, apparel, transportation, medical care, recreation, education and communication, other goods and services) plus special aggregates (core/"all items less food and energy," energy, commodities vs. services, etc.).

**Data types:**
- Index levels (base 1982-84=100 for CPI-U), monthly percent changes, 12-month changes, seasonally adjusted and unadjusted series (indexes published to three decimal places since 2007).
- Annual and semiannual average indexes.
- **Relative importance weights** and "aspects" metadata (e.g., end-of-year relative importance, item contributions to change).
- **Average price data** for selected items: utility (piped) gas, electricity, gasoline (all types), and select foods (e.g., milk, eggs, ground beef, bread). Average prices are published for the U.S. city average and select areas.
- Historical depth: continuous monthly national data from **1913**; some food-only estimates even earlier; metro-area series begin later (varies by area).

**Sample scale:** Approximately **80,000–100,000 price quotes per month**, collected in **75 urban areas** from about **23,000 retail/service establishments** and ~6,000 housing units (rent) — one of the largest ongoing primary data collections in the federal government. Prices are collected by BLS economic assistants in person, by phone, and increasingly from websites/apps (alternative data collection).

## 5. Methodology (Summary)

- **Two-stage design**: (1) *basic indexes* for ~7,776 item-area combinations, calculated mostly with a **geometric mean formula** (partly modified Laspeyres); (2) *aggregation* to published indexes using expenditure weights from the **Consumer Expenditure Survey (CE)** — weights are now updated annually (e.g., 2021 CE data set the weights effective end-2022).
- **Housing**: rents and owners' equivalent rent estimated from a survey of residential units (owners' equivalent rent since 1983 replaced the earlier asset-approach treatment of homeownership).
- **Quality adjustment**: hedonic regression for goods/services with rapidly changing quality (computers, apparel, appliances); direct quality adjustment where feasible.
- **Sampling rotation**: outlets and items rotated regularly; geographic sample rotated each decade based on the census (current design from 2018).
- **Seasonal adjustment**: X-13ARIMA-SEATS; seasonal factors recalculated annually with concurrent revision of up to 5 years of seasonally adjusted history (the only routine "revision" to CPI-U/CPI-W).
- **Full documentation**: *BLS Handbook of Methods, Chapter 17* (bls.gov/opub/hom/cpi/home.htm) — a model of transparent methodology documentation, plus technical notes attached to each news release.

## 6. Users and Uses

**Policy and government users:**
- **Federal Reserve** — the CPI (especially core CPI) is a key input to monetary policy (targeting PCE inflation but watching CPI closely); monthly releases move markets within seconds.
- **Social Security Administration** — automatic annual COLAs computed from the CPI-W (Q3 average vs. prior peak). Over **67 million beneficiaries** are affected.
- **SNAP/USDA** and school lunch programs — benefit adjustments and eligibility thresholds tied to CPI; over **41 million SNAP recipients** affected.
- **IRS/Treasury** — tax brackets, standard deduction, and many other tax parameters indexed to the Chained CPI since 2018 (CPI-U before that).
- **Treasury** — TIPS principal and Series I savings bond rates are indexed to the NSA CPI-U.
- Per BLS: the CPI affects the income of **more than 108 million people** through statutory indexation alone.

**Private-sector users:** collective bargaining agreements with CPI escalators; commercial and residential rent escalation clauses; alimony, child support, and royalty adjustments; corporate planning and pricing; actuarial work (pension COLAs); the inflation-derivatives market (CPI swaps).

**Research/media/public:** economists, think tanks, journalists, courts (inflation-adjusting legal awards), students, and the general public via the widely used **BLS CPI Inflation Calculator**.

**Canonical uses enumerated by BLS:** (1) economic indicator of inflation, (2) deflator of other economic series (real wages, real retail sales, some NIPA components), (3) means of adjusting dollar values (income payments, eligibility levels, tax structure).

## 7. Benefits to the Public

- **Automatic, rule-based protection from inflation** for the elderly, disabled, low-income households, and veterans — no annual political renegotiation required.
- **Prevention of "bracket creep"** — inflation no longer silently pushes taxpayers into higher brackets.
- **A common, neutral yardstick** for millions of private contracts, reducing disputes and transaction costs.
- **Macro steering** — credible, independent inflation measurement underpins monetary policy credibility and inflation expectations.
- **Real-value analysis** — deflating wages, earnings, and GDP components to distinguish real from nominal change; the public's shared measure of "what a dollar is worth."
- **Transparency and accountability** — free, documented, reproducible data; methodology is open, and changes are announced and explained in advance.

## 8. Limitations, Criticisms, and Controversies

Every user should know these — the CPI is statistically contested and politically charged:

- **Not a true cost-of-living index (COLI)** — it approximates one; the Stigler Committee (1961) and Boskin Commission (1996) both pressed this point.
- **Substitution bias**: a fixed-basket approach overstates inflation when consumers switch to cheaper alternatives. Addressed at the basic level by the geometric mean formula (1999) and fully by the C-CPI-U (2002) — the C-CPI-U typically runs ~0.2–0.3 pp/year lower.
- **Quality change and new-goods bias**: the hardest measurement problem. Hedonic adjustment is technically contested; critics argue the CPI either over- or under-states inflation depending on the treatment of quality improvements (e.g., healthcare).
- **The Boskin controversy**: the claim of ~1.1 pp/year upward bias implied large Social Security savings; critics (including BLS leadership — see Moulton & Moses 1997 and BLS's formal response) argued the estimate rested on unverifiable judgment. Politically, the episode is remembered as an attempt to cut benefits by statistical means, and it made CPI methodology permanently politicized.
- **Chained CPI politics**: proposals to switch Social Security COLAs to the slower-growing C-CPI-U (e.g., the 2013 Obama "Grand Bargain" offer; the 2018 tax-bracket switch) are recurring budget flashpoints; AARP and other advocates oppose the switch as a benefit cut.
- **CPI-E debate**: advocates argue Social Security should use an elderly-weighted index (healthcare-heavy); BLS publishes R-CPI-E but cautions that its expenditure weights, outlets, and items have significant limitations and it is not designed for indexation.
- **Coverage gaps**: urban-only (~93% of population); no official subpopulation inflation rates; metro-level series are volatile with wide confidence intervals.
- **Weight lag**: weights reflect CE data collected 1–2 years earlier — during rapid inflation regime shifts (2021–22), BLS accelerated annual weight updates in response.
- **Accuracy/precision**: BLS publishes standard errors and has a standing research program on CPI accuracy (see "Assessing and improving the accuracy of the CPI," *Monthly Labor Review*, 2024).
- **No routine revisions**: by policy, CPI-U and CPI-W are final at release (revisions would be costly to escalation contracts); only seasonal factors are revised. The C-CPI-U is the exception (three quarterly revisions before final).

## 9. Data Access, Formats, and Technical Details

**For data scientists and librarians:**

- **Series ID anatomy**: e.g., `CUUR0000SA0` = CPI program (C), All Urban Consumers (U), Not Seasonally Adjusted (U), area code `0000` (U.S. city average), item code `SA0` (All items), base period code (R = 1982-84=100). `CUSR0000SA0` is the seasonally adjusted counterpart; CPI-W series use `CW...`; C-CPI-U uses `SUUR...`. Flat-file "mapping" tables (cu.item, cu.area, cu.series, cu.seasonal, etc.) decode every component.
- **Bulk flat files**: https://download.bls.gov/pub/time.series/cu/ (CPI-U) and /cw/ (CPI-W) — free, no registration, tab-delimited, full-history text files partitioned by category, plus mapping files and the newer `cu.aspect` metadata file (relative importance and other per-series aspects). A ~50 MB current data file plus category partitions; ideal for harvesting/archiving.
- **BLS Public Data API v2**: `https://api.bls.gov/publicAPI/v2/timeseries/data/` — JSON and Excel output; unregistered queries limited to 25 series/3 years (daily limits); free registration key raises limits to 50 series/20 years; supports calculations, annual averages, catalog, and aspects options.
- **Other channels**: CPI Databases (one-screen/multi-screen data tools) on bls.gov/cpi/data; monthly news release HTML/text and time-series `ts` files (text-format releases at https://www.bls.gov/news.release/cpi.toc.htm and /release/cpi.txt); FRED (St. Louis Fed) mirrors headline series (e.g., CPIAUCSL, CPIAUCNS) with easy API access; Data.gov catalog entries; BLS Public Data API SDKs in R, Python, SAS, etc.
- **Reference month concept and seasonal adjustment** must be understood to avoid common analytical errors; the FAQ (bls.gov/cpi/questions-and-answers.htm) and technical notes in every release explain the conventions.
- **Citation formats** are provided by BLS; data are public domain (U.S. federal government work).

**For preservationists:**

- **No vintage/version archive is officially maintained for microdata** — individual price quotes are confidential under CIPSEA and never published. The preservable artifact is the aggregate time series and documentation.
- **Key archival resources**: the BLS *Handbook of Methods* chapter (with archived prior versions, e.g., /archive/20230906/ — BLS retains superseded methodology versions, which is excellent practice); the "Chronology of changes" page; CPI-U-RS research series (a historically consistent re-estimation, 1978–present); historical news releases retained on bls.gov; **FRASER** (Federal Reserve Archival System for Economic Research, fraser.stlouisfed.org) archives BLS bulletins and price series back to the 19th century, including the WWI-era cost-of-living studies; NBER's historical price series compilations extend coverage back into the 1800s.
- **Risks**: URL rot and site redesigns (BLS has migrated file structures over the years — the `blsmon1.bls.gov` mirrors seen in search results are an artifact of such changes); methodology versioning is documented but scattered across Handbook archives, factsheets, and MLR articles; flat files are regenerated in place (so archival snapshots of download.bls.gov preserve vintages).

## 10. Quick Reference: Key Facts at a Glance

| Question | Answer |
|---|---|
| Publisher | U.S. Bureau of Labor Statistics (Dept. of Labor) |
| Authority | 29 U.S.C. §§1–2 (general BLS statistical authority); downstream statutes (42 U.S.C. §415(i), IRC §1(f)) mandate its use |
| First data | 1913 (national), continuous monthly |
| Frequency | Monthly |
| Population covered | CPI-U ≈ 93% of U.S. population (urban) |
| Sample | ~80,000 prices/month; 75 areas; ~23,000 establishments + ~6,000 housing units |
| Headline series | CPI-U All Items, U.S. city average, SA and NSA |
| Revisions | CPI-U/CPI-W final at release (seasonal factors revised annually); C-CPI-U revised quarterly up to 3 times |
| Cost | Free, public domain |
| People affected by statutory use | 108+ million |

## 11. Principal Sources Consulted

- BLS CPI program pages: overview, methodology, FAQ, technical notes (bls.gov/cpi)
- BLS Handbook of Methods, Ch. 17, Consumer Price Index — design, calculation, data sources, presentation, history (bls.gov/opub/hom/cpi)
- "Chronology of changes in the Consumer Price Index" (bls.gov/cpi/additional-resources/historical-changes.htm)
- "The first hundred years of the Consumer Price Index" and "One hundred years of price change," *Monthly Labor Review* (2014); "Assessing and improving the accuracy of the CPI," MLR (2024)
- 29 U.S.C. Chapter 1, Subchapter I (uscode.house.gov), including the CPI-E mandate at Pub. L. 100-175 §191
- Boskin Commission Final Report (Senate Finance Committee print 104-72, Dec. 1996); BLS response (Moulton & Moses 1997; gj10.pdf); NBER w12311
- CRS reports on Social Security COLAs (94-803; IF12675) and CBO budget options on chained CPI
- BLS Public Data API v2 documentation; download.bls.gov time-series flat files; CPI aspect-metadata factsheet

**Bottom line:** The CPI is among the most consequential, longest-running, and best-documented datasets in the federal statistical system — free, methodologically transparent, and directly touching the incomes of over 100 million Americans — but it is also a dataset whose methodology and choice of variant (CPI-U vs. CPI-W vs. Chained) carry multi-billion-dollar policy stakes, which every serious user should understand before working with it.

### Historical Data Availability
- Gone: Data files prior to the current year or cycle are no longer publicly available.
- High Risk: Some data files prior to the current year or cycle are removed.
- Moderate Risk: Some data elements that exist in the dataset prior to the current year or cycle are removed.
- No Known Issue: Data prior to the current year or cycle remain accessible with no known alterations.

### Future Data Availability
- Gone: Data collection and publication has been terminated.
- High Risk: Statutory publication deadline missed and/or collection or publication skipped and/or ICR expired for more than one year.
- Moderate Risk: Typical or intended publication date missed and/or collection or publication delayed; ICR expired up to one year.
- No Known Issue: Data published on time or as expected and ICR active or renewed before expiration.

### Data Quality
- Gone: Data collection and publication has been terminated.
- High Risk: Reductions in granularity, timeliness, or frequency.
- Moderate Risk: Potential or emerging risk to granularity, timeliness, or frequency.
- No Known Issue: Maintained or improved granularity, timeliness, or frequency.

- High Risk: Statutory authorization is vague and/or there are alternative data collections that could serve as substitutes and/or no known programmatic use.

- No Known Issue: Statutorily required and/or statutory authorization is explicitly named and it is clear what has to be collected, and there aren't alternative data collections that could serve as substitutes and/or required for implementation of a federal program.

### Staffing and Funding

**Assessment date:** October 2026. Research draws on BLS program notices, OMB/reginfo ICR records, the American Statistical Association's (ASA) *The Nation's Data at Risk* report, Federal Register notices, and press coverage (AP, Reuters, NYT, CNN, Bloomberg, Politico). Note: the USAJobs staffing tracker (usajobs-tracker.abigailhaddad.com) was itself archived on **December 31, 2025** and its data table is JavaScript-rendered, so I could not extract agency-level figures directly from it; I have relied on ASA's staffing estimates instead, which are corroborated by press reporting.

**Timeline of key events since January 2025:**

- **Feb 2025** — DOGE established at DOL; ~2,700 DOL staff (~20% of the department) depart via deferred resignations/early retirements (The Guardian, May 2025)
- **Feb–Mar 2025** — BLS technical and data-user advisory committees and the Federal Economic Statistics Advisory Committee (FESAC) disbanded pursuant to a Feb. 19, 2025 executive order (Politico, Mar 2025)
- **April/June 2025** — BLS suspends CPI data collection entirely in Lincoln, NE and Provo, UT (April) and Buffalo, NY (June); ~15% of the sample in the other 72 collection areas also suspended (~19% of total collection suspended as of June) (BLS notice, June 2025)
- **June 2025** — FY2026 President's Budget proposes ~8% cut to BLS budget and staffing, prioritizing only Principal Federal Economic Indicators (Bloomberg)
- **Aug 1, 2025** — President Trump fires BLS Commissioner Erika McEntarfer, publicly alleging (without evidence) that jobs data were "rigged"; Deputy Commissioner William Wiatrowski becomes acting commissioner (AP, Reuters, Politico)
- **Oct 1–Nov 12, 2025** — Government shutdown halts CPI collection; September CPI released 9 days late (Oct 24, 2025); **October 2025 CPI release canceled entirely** (announced Nov 21, 2025) — no all-items or core index for October 2025; November CPI published Dec 18, 2025; December CPI published Jan 13, 2026 on the original schedule (BLS shutdown notices, Reuters)
- **Aug 19, 2026** — BLS submits ICR renewal (202604-1220-001, OMB No. 1220-0039) to OIRA ahead of the Oct 31, 2026 expiration; the request documents a burden **reduction of ~43,982 annual responses**, partly because "adjustments have been made to bring workload into parity with staffing levels" (reginfo.gov, omb.report, 91 FR 53664)

## Category-by-Category Assessment

### 1. Historical Data Availability

**Evidence by level:**
- *Gone*: No evidence. Historical CPI time series (1913–present) remain fully available at download.bls.gov, through the BLS API, and mirrored by FRED (CPIAUCSL, etc.) and FRASER (which archives BLS bulletins and even the 2025 shutdown-affected release text).
- *High Risk*: No evidence that pre-2025/2026 data files have been removed from bls.gov or the bulk download repository.
- *Moderate Risk*: No evidence of removal of historical data elements. One caveat: Buffalo, Lincoln, and Provo metro-area indexes continue to be published but are now sustained by imputation rather than direct collection, increasing their volatility; this is a prospective quality issue, not a removal.
- *No Known Issue*: All historical files (flat files, series, mapping tables, Handbook of Methods archives, historical news releases) remain accessible without known alteration. BLS even preserved detailed documentation of the October 2025 gap rather than backfilling it.

**Selected level: No Known Issue** — with the important caveat that the **October 2025 gap is a permanent hole in the historical record** (headline and core CPI, plus most item and area indexes, were never published for that month, and BLS states it "cannot provide specific guidance to data users for navigating the missing October observations"). This is a forward-looking data-integrity problem, not a removal of previously published data.

### 2. Future Data Availability

**Evidence by level:**
- *Gone*: No evidence — publication continues (Dec 2025 CPI released on schedule Jan 13, 2026).
- *High Risk*: **The October 2025 CPI collection was skipped entirely and the October 2025 release was canceled** (BLS: "BLS did not publish an all items or an all items less food and energy estimate for October 2025"; Reuters, Nov 21, 2025). The rubric explicitly defines "collection or publication skipped" as High Risk.
- *Moderate Risk*: September 2025 CPI published 9 days late (Oct 15 → Oct 24, 2025) to allow SSA to meet statutory COLA deadlines; November CPI published 11 days late (Dec 18, 2025). ICR active: extension request (202604-1220-001) submitted to OIRA Aug 19, 2026, before the Oct 31, 2026 expiration, following proper 60-day (91 FR 23311) and 30-day (91 FR 53664) Federal Register notices.
- *No Known Issue*: Not supportable given the October cancellation.

**Selected level: High Risk** — the October 2025 skip plainly meets the rubric's High Risk trigger ("collection or publication skipped"). Mitigating context: the skip was caused by a lapse in appropriations (an external event), not a programmatic decision to discontinue; BLS resumed on-schedule publication immediately after the shutdown; and the ICR is being renewed on time. However, the same resource constraints that drove the shutdown-era vulnerability (staffing losses, collection suspensions) remain in place, so the risk of recurrence cannot be discounted.

### 3. Data Quality

**Evidence by level:**
- *Gone*: No evidence — the CPI is still produced monthly.
- *High Risk*: Substantial documented reductions in granularity: collection suspended entirely in 3 metro areas; ~15% of the sample suspended across the other 72 areas (~19% of total collection as of June 2025); BLS's own notice states these actions "may increase the volatility of subnational or item-specific indexes," and the number of imputed prices rose (CNN noted imputed-price share jumped ~15% in March 2025). The 2026 ICR renewal documents a permanent ~44,000-response (~14%) reduction in annual collection burden explicitly attributed to bringing "workload into parity with staffing levels." October 2025 indexes were computed entirely from carry-forward imputation, and 1-month changes for November 2025 were suppressed where October data are missing. ASA's report states BLS "has had to suspend data collection for the CPI in some parts of the country" as a direct result of staff and budget constraints.
- *Moderate Risk*: Would apply if these were only prospective; they are already realized.
- *No Known Issue*: Not supportable — BLS itself published notices flagging increased volatility, and CRS issued a 2025 report titled "The Consumer Price Index: Data Quality."

**Selected level: High Risk** — reductions in granularity (geographic and item-level sample, imputation rates) have already occurred, are formally documented by BLS, and are being institutionalized through the reduced ICR workload. BLS's own simulation shows the impact on the national all-items index is minimal (<0.01 pp average), which protects the headline figure, but subnational and item-level granularity has demonstrably degraded.

### 4. Statutory Context

**Evidence by level:**
- *Gone*: N/A per rubric.
- *High Risk*: Would require vague authorization, available substitutes, or no programmatic use — none of which hold. One nuance: the CPI rests on BLS's *general* authority (29 U.S.C. §2, "collect, collate, and report at least once each year" statistics on labor conditions) rather than a CPI-specific collection mandate — a partial point of vagueness.
- *Moderate Risk*: Would apply if the CPI were required for program implementation but with available substitutes. PCE (BEA) and PPI exist as alternative inflation measures, but **no substitute can perform the CPI's statutory functions**: Social Security COLAs must by statute (42 U.S.C. §415(i)) be computed from the CPI-W; IRC §1(f) requires the Chained CPI for tax-bracket indexation; TIPS and Series I bonds are indexed to the CPI-U. During the shutdown, BLS explicitly prioritized the September CPI release so SSA could meet "statutory deadlines necessary to ensure the accurate and timely payment of benefits" — demonstrating the binding statutory linkage in practice.
- *No Known Issue*: The CPI is explicitly named in statute as the index for multiple mandatory federal program adjustments, is a designated Principal Federal Economic Indicator (OMB Circular A-11), and no alternative collection can substitute for these uses. The ICR record names 29 U.S.C. §2 as the authorizing statute and the collection is OMB-approved.

**Selected level: No Known Issue** — the CPI has the strongest possible statutory anchoring of essentially any federal dataset: it is the operative index for Social Security COLAs, tax indexation, and inflation-protected securities. The 2025–26 turmoil never threatened termination precisely because these statutory dependencies make the CPI politically untouchable as a *program*, even as its inputs are squeezed. (The residual "vagueness" in collection authority is what allowed the administration latitude to shrink the *sample* without statutory amendment.)

### 5. Staffing and Funding

**Evidence by level:**
- *Gone*: No evidence — BLS continues to operate.
- *High Risk*: **Leadership removed**: President Trump fired Senate-confirmed BLS Commissioner Erika McEntarfer on Aug 1, 2025, after publicly attacking the data as "rigged"; the agency has since been led by an acting commissioner (AP, Reuters, The Hill). ASA estimates **BLS lost ~22% of staffing since FY24** (2,058 FTE baseline). DOL overall lost ~20% of its workforce (~2,700 staff) before any formal RIF (The Guardian). FY26 President's Budget proposed ~8% cuts to BLS budget and staffing (Bloomberg; DOL budget documents). DOGE targeted 87 DOL office closures and ~96 contract terminations (Bloomberg Law).
- *Moderate Risk*: The 22% staff loss falls in the 10–39% band; BLS staff loss in absolute terms (~450) is below the 500 threshold; proposed budget cut (~8%) is below 10%. But the leadership-removal trigger is independently satisfied.
- *No Known Issue*: Not supportable.

**Selected level: High Risk** — the removal of the agency head via public presidential intervention, combined with >20% staff attrition, clearly satisfies the High Risk criteria ("leadership removed"). Caveats: the BLS budget cut *proposed* in FY26 (~8%) alone would be Moderate; the final FY26 appropriation outcome for BLS could not be confirmed from available sources (my appropriations search was constrained), so the budget component of this rating rests on the proposal and reported constraints. Note also that BLS staffing losses are attrition-driven (deferred resignations, hiring freezes, contract cuts to data-collection contractors) rather than a single mass RIF.

### 6. Policy

**Evidence by level:**
- *Gone*: No evidence — publication continues.
- *High Risk*: Significant changes in accordance with Administration priorities have occurred: (a) resource-driven CPI collection reductions announced with explicit justification that "current resources can no longer support the collection effort"; (b) the President's public campaign against BLS data veracity ("RIGGED") and the retaliatory firing of the commissioner — creating a documented climate of political pressure on the agency (Reuters: "firing your chief statistician is a dangerous step"; PolitiFact: "baseless"); (c) disbandment of the advisory committees (FESAC, BLS technical and data user committees) that provided external quality oversight; (d) ASA concludes BLS "has been buffeted by the Administration's actions to oust the commissioner and cast doubt on the veracity of BLS estimates."
- *Moderate Risk*: Would apply if changes were merely proposed or signaled. Here, the collection reductions, committee disbandments, and leadership purge have all already been executed.
- *No Known Issue*: Not supportable — multiple significant changes since January 2025.
- Note on the "Presidential Action-driven ICR" prong: I found no evidence that the CPI ICR itself (OMB No. 1220-0039) was directed by presidential action; the Aug 2026 renewal is a routine "extension without change of a currently approved collection." The High Risk rating rests on the "other significant changes in accordance with Administration priorities" prong.

**Selected level: High Risk** — the direction of policy pressure (staffing cuts → sample cuts → imputation increases) is aligned with administration downsizing priorities, and the politicization of BLS leadership is unprecedented for a federal statistical agency. Important counterweight: BLS's *substantive* conduct has remained professionally orthodox — it refused to retroactively fabricate October data, used only pre-existing documented imputation methods, published transparent notices of every reduction, and maintained that no methodology change was made without Federal Register process. The risk is environmental and resource-driven, not (so far) a manipulation of published figures.

---

## Overall Risk Summary

Historical Data Availability: **No Known Issue**
Future Data Availability: **High Risk**
Data Quality: **High Risk**
Statutory Context: **No Known Issue**
Staffing and Funding: **High Risk**
Policy: **High Risk**

**Narrative synthesis:** The CPI sits in an unusual position: it is simultaneously among the *least* likely federal datasets to be terminated (ironclad statutory dependencies — Social Security COLAs, tax indexation, TIPS — make it a Principal Federal Economic Indicator the administration itself prioritized protecting in its budget) and among the *most* affected in terms of degraded inputs and institutional stress. The realized harm to date is concentrated in (1) a permanent one-month hole in the historical series (October 2025), (2) reduced geographic/item-level sample and elevated imputation, and (3) a destabilized agency (fired commissioner, ~22% staff loss, disbanded oversight committees). Headline national indexes have so far been preserved with demonstrably minimal bias (per BLS's own simulation), but the sample reductions are being locked in through the 2026 ICR, and the risk of another shutdown-driven gap or further collection cuts remains elevated. For preservation purposes, users should treat bls.gov bulk files and FRED/FRASER mirrors as currently intact, but should snapshot vintages given the demonstrated fragility exposed in 2025.
